sources.note: Tambotalo is listed among languages showing the labial > dental/apico-labial shift (lower case = dental reflexes, i.e. Tambotalo has dentals, not linguolabials). The words stress/accent/tone do not occur in the paper. Nothing on Tambotalo prosody.

sources.citation: Guy, Jacques B. M. 1981. Glottochronology without cognate recognition. Pacific Linguistics B-79. viii+142 pp. Canberra: Research School of Pacific Studies, ANU. doi:10.15144/PL-B79 (ANU record dated 1980)
sources.note: Only segmental/comparative remarks: Tolomako 'has dentals as reflexes of *p and *m preceding front vowels (Guy 1978). This particular sound change is found only in two South Santo languages (Roria and Tambotalo), in all the NE Santo languages, and in an intermediate stage.. in most offshore island languages'; 'Tambotalo is classified with Tangoa on the basis of proportions of shared cognates, whereas, on the basis of (X2-b)/N measurements, it is given as having split early from an offshore island subgroup Mafea-Tutuba-Aore-Malo.' The only 'stress placement' in the book (p.1) is a hypothetical…

sources.citation: Guy, Jacques B. M. 1978. Proto-North New Hebridean reconstructions. In S. A. Wurm & L. Carrington (eds), Second International Conference on Austronesian Linguistics: Proceedings, 781-850. Pacific Linguistics C-61. Canberra: ANU. doi:10.15144/PL-C61.781
sources.note: p.782: 'Word-stress does not seem to have existed in PNNH as it appears to have been innovated along different rules in Sakao, Lehali, and Shark Bay'; Sakao 'Stage 2. Word-stress is innovated.. stress most often affected the penultimate syllable'. Tambotalo appears only as a reflex citation ('If we reconstruct pila, we expect Tambotalo (64) ndrila and Aore pila'). No statement about Tambotalo stress.
